meta.title: TeamHaim training plan rules
meta.purpose: Every rule a training plan must follow, distilled from all 18 chapters and the four protocols of the brain. The season writer gets all of them; the rules marked enforced_by 'code' are checked again after the plan is written and can only make it safer (lower volume, fewer workouts, easier days).
meta.sourcing: Rules are written in TeamHaim's own words. The training science behind them is credited to Marius Bakken, 'The Norwegian Method'; source_chapters lists where each comes from. Rules with no chapter are TeamHaim's own.

enforced_by.code: checked in athlete_api.py after the plan is written
enforced_by.plan: the season writer must follow it
enforced_by.coach: used by the coach in chat and run feedback

rules.rule: All threshold work is done below the threshold (the Golden Zone), never at or above it.
rules.why: The method's volume only works if the muscles can absorb it; just above threshold the muscular cost jumps disproportionately.

rules.rule: Every easy run stays below 70% of max heart rate, the whole run, at every level.
rules.why: Easy days exist to lower muscle tone; the grey zone between easy and threshold costs load without the benefit.

rules.rule: Golden Zone pace depends on rep length: short reps at T-pace to +7 s/km, medium +7 to +14, long +14 to +21 s/km slower.
rules.why: Longer reps must run slower to stay under the threshold for the whole rep.

rules.rule: Start the first rep 5-7 s/km slower than target and build through the session; never make the first or last rep the hardest.
rules.why: A soft start leaves room to adjust if the body isn't responding that day.

rules.rule: When in doubt, run slower. Paces from calculators or watches get a margin below them (watch thresholds often read 3-5% too high).
rules.why: Threshold shifts with sleep, stress, heat and fatigue; a few seconds too fast turns a controlled week into a lost one.

rules.rule: Runners new to threshold training start with a conservative Golden Zone (below about 3.0 mmol/L) for their first months.
rules.why: An adaptation period lets untrained muscles catch up before the zone is pushed.

rules.rule: A green-light day means adding reps, never adding speed.
rules.why: Receptive days are for more volume in the zone, not for crossing it.

rules.rule: Pace adjustments inside a session are small: 2-5 s/km, not 10+.
rules.why: Needing a big change means the day or the setup is off; change the session instead of forcing it.

rules.rule: Workouts per week follow run days: 3 run days -> 1 workout; 4-5 -> 2; 6 or more -> up to 3 (the third, the X-session, is optional). Every other run is easy or the long run.
rules.why: The three key sessions only work when all other runs are genuinely easy, and hard days need easy days between them.

rules.rule: Never two hard days back to back. The main threshold session has an easy day before and after it.
rules.why: Muscle tone peaks the day after a hard session; the easy day lets it drop before the next one.

rules.rule: Easy days are protected: no speed work, strength or drills on them.
rules.why: Anything extra on an easy day keeps tone up, so the next quality session starts heavy.

rules.rule: The main threshold session (long reps, 10+ min, or varied continuous running for marathoners) happens at most once a week.
rules.why: It's the week's highest-load session and too demanding to repeat.

rules.rule: The support session uses short reps: up to 3 minutes (occasionally 6), often 45/15.
rules.why: Short reps give quality time in the zone at lower cost, balancing the main session.

rules.rule: The X-session is optional and the first thing cut at any sign of overload or injury.
rules.why: It's the spice, not the base; the two threshold sessions carry the plan.

rules.rule: Vary rep length across the week and from week to week (short, medium, long); don't repeat one session type all the time.
rules.why: Variation prevents plateaus; sticking to one interval length is the most common mistake.

rules.rule: Keep weeks simple and similar; complexity belongs in the season's phases, not inside one week.
rules.why: Predictable weeks mean predictable muscle tone and fewer risky transitions.

rules.rule: With 4-6 hours a week, aim for roughly 60-65% easy, 20-30% Golden Zone and 5-10% above threshold.
rules.why: The 80/20 split was measured on elites training 15-25 hours; at low hours it leaves too little quality time.

rules.rule: Under time pressure, keep at least one threshold session a week and never go more than a week without one.
rules.why: A minimum dose keeps the adaptations alive through busy periods.

rules.rule: A missed quality session is not made up later; the plan moves on.
rules.why: Squeezing it in breaks the easy days that protect the next sessions.

rules.rule: Very long reps (11-20 min) appear at most once every 10-14 days.
rules.why: They're easy to start too hard and turn into a fight against lactate.

rules.rule: Week 1 of a season starts where the athlete is now: at most 5% above their recent weekly average.
rules.why: Transitions in load are when injuries happen; the season shouldn't open with one.

rules.rule: A build week rises at most 10% (and at most 8 km) over the build week before it.
rules.why: Gradual increases let tendons and muscles keep up with the heart and lungs, which adapt faster.

rules.rule: No single run grows more than about 10% beyond the athlete's longest run of the last few weeks, and none is ever double it.
rules.why: Injury risk tracks single-session spikes more than weekly totals; doubling the longest recent run sharply raises it.

rules.rule: Volume never goes above the athlete's weekly goal; without one, never above their biggest week of the past year (or 20% above now).
rules.why: More kilometres help only if the body absorbs them; the athlete's life and goal set the ceiling.

rules.rule: If the athlete wants to keep their kilometres, weeks stay within 5% of them and progress comes from the sessions.
rules.why: Many runners improve for a long time on threshold quality alone.

rules.rule: When volume rises, only the easy runs grow. The quality sessions stay the same size.
rules.why: Quality sessions are the priority and are never traded for kilometres.

rules.rule: Never raise volume and intensity at the same time; structure first, then volume, then (only if needed) intensity.
rules.why: Changing two loads at once is the classic path to overload.

rules.rule: A top-up block of about 6 weeks at roughly +10% a week can build toward a race, finishing about 4 weeks before it.
rules.why: Gradual extra easy volume before a goal race gives a lift at low risk.

rules.rule: For 5K and 10K goals the long run is 60-90 minutes of easy running; for half and full marathon it builds progressively week by week.
rules.why: Short-race athletes need the aerobic volume, not the extra mechanical load of very long runs.

rules.rule: The long run is fully easy (below 70% max HR). A long run with 45/15 at the end counts as a hard day and is followed by an easy day.
rules.why: The combination is loading enough on its own.

rules.rule: The day after a hill session or the X-session is an easy, slightly longer run (60-90 minutes lowers tone well).
rules.why: Easy distance after hard hill work brings muscle tone down fastest.

rules.rule: Double threshold is for athletes training about 6+ hours a week. Recreational runners: none or one double day a week; ambitious: up to two; never beginners.
rules.why: It works because intensity stays controlled; without a solid base it becomes two hard sessions in one day.

rules.rule: Morning session: longer reps, run clearly slower (expect 10-15 s/km slower than the evening's short reps). Evening: shorter reps, same effort, never pushed harder because it feels good.
rules.why: Longer reps in the morning keep tone from climbing all day; lower evening lactate means receptive, not permission to speed up.

rules.rule: 6-8 hours between the two sessions (2-3 hours can work; over 10-12 they become two separate sessions).
rules.why: The body treats the pair as one block when they sit inside the receptive window.

rules.rule: At least one easy day between double days, and at first the days after (and before) a double day are completely easy.
rules.why: The stress response peaks the day after, which must stay easy.

rules.rule: Build into it in steps: easy run AM + threshold PM for 4-6 weeks first, and keep each session to 15-20 minutes of work at the start.
rules.why: A gradual entry avoids the most common error: two sessions that are both a little too hard.

rules.rule: No double threshold on physically demanding workdays; rest between the sessions.
rules.why: Standing or physical work between sessions raises muscular load and injury risk.

rules.rule: Work above the threshold stays small: under about 30 minutes a week for ambitious athletes, only when fully recovered; at 4-6 hours a week no extra hard sessions beyond the X-session.
rules.why: Intense work costs far more recovery and can switch the body toward anaerobic habits too early.

rules.rule: 45/15 or other hard reps never go the day after a hard session.
rules.why: They need fresh legs to be done well.

rules.rule: Hills (when the athlete has one) are the X-session in the build phase; closer to racing they alternate with flat race-pace work, then give way to race-specific sessions.
rules.why: Uphill running is built-in strength work at lower speed and lower injury risk.

rules.rule: Race-pace work is regulated by rest and rep length, not by running faster.
rules.why: You get kilometres at race pace while keeping the overall effort near threshold.

rules.rule: An easier week every 4th week (every 3rd when returning from a break or injury; alternating in short blocks): at least 20% fewer kilometres and one fewer workout.
rules.why: The lighter week should lift performance above the weeks before it, not just rest.

rules.rule: Every change is gradual: phases, surfaces, shoes, adding a new session type. Allow weeks, not days, to move between phases.
rules.why: Transitions are where injuries come from.

rules.rule: New to the method: a flat, threshold-only structure first (threshold sessions plus easy running); add 45/15 or an X-session only once that's absorbed and injury-free.
rules.why: A stable base normalizes the muscles before variation and intensity are added.
rules.applies_to: beginners and athletes new to the method

rules.rule: Check progress at least every 4 weeks and adjust paces and load to what the body is doing.
rules.why: Performance should rise through the hard weeks and come back stronger after the easier ones.

rules.rule: In the racing season, two threshold sessions a week are enough: the goal is maintenance plus race-specific work.
rules.why: Keeping the threshold base is what speed is built on; losing it can't be fixed by speed alone.

rules.rule: The final two weeks cut volume but keep the number of sessions; sessions get shorter, not faster.
rules.why: Muscles need to stay active while the body rests; race form is mostly muscular state on the day.

rules.rule: In race week: a sharper session about 4 days out and a short threshold session about 2 days out.
rules.why: This steers muscle tone toward its best on race day.

rules.rule: Taper weeks never go up in volume.
rules.why: Taper is for arriving fresh.

rules.rule: Returning from a break or injury: same structure, threshold time capped at 20-25 minutes per session, and volume only rises after the body has re-adapted.
rules.why: Choose the structure first and increase volume second, never the reverse.

rules.rule: Fever or symptoms below the neck: no running. Mild symptoms above the neck: at most 10-15 minutes of easy jogging and a few strides.
rules.why: Training through a fever risks a long setback.

rules.rule: Coming back after illness: 2-3 short-rep sessions (30/30, 45/15) a week for two weeks, just under threshold, while rebuilding volume.
rules.why: Short reps restore muscle elasticity quickly at low risk.

rules.rule: If an injury is suspected, stop the session and take one to two days off.
rules.why: Early stops prevent long breaks.

rules.rule: Signs of overload (heavy stairs, waking at 3-5 am, no good session in 10 days, rising effort at the same pace): cut intensity, not volume; keep most runs around 70% max HR with a little 45/15.
rules.why: Easy running helps muscles normalize; complete rest often makes the return harder.

rules.rule: Achilles, calf or foot problems: no hill running until pain-free.
rules.why: Uphill running loads the Achilles and calf hardest (a TeamHaim safety rule).

rules.rule: Strength work only when there's a reason (over 50, bone-stress history, recurring injury, plateau); most healthy runners under 40 don't need it.
rules.why: It raises muscle tone and eats into threshold volume.

rules.rule: When it's in: 1-2 short sessions a week for 6-12 weeks, then 1 to maintain; heavy-ish, eccentric-focused (hamstrings, calves), about 80% of an 'ideal' program; placed right after a threshold session, not on easy days.
rules.why: Minimum effective dose at the lowest cost to the running.

rules.rule: Very little cross-training in the plan; running-specific load is what adapts runners.
rules.why: Adaptation to load is running-specific.

rules.rule: New shoes: start with 20-30% of weekly volume in them, then add 10-15% a week.
rules.why: A shoe change is a load transition like any other.

rules.rule: Kilometres only, paces in min/km; miles are converted (1 mile = 1.60934 km).
rules.why: One unit everywhere prevents mistakes.

rules.rule: Distances are whole kilometres (8 km, not 8.3 km).
rules.why: Plans should be easy to read and follow.

rules.rule: Explain the plan like a coach: why these sessions and these kilometres suit this athlete and their goal. Don't show the athlete rule names or 'safety checks'.
rules.why: The athlete should understand and trust the plan; the rules are the coach's tools.
